why: The textbook 0-1 BFS: every move costs either 0 (along an arrow) or 1 (against it). A deque replaces Dijkstra's heap: 0-cost neighbours go to the front and 1-cost neighbours to the back, so vertices still come out in order of distance, in O(V + E).
hints: Turn each directed edge u -> v into two undirected moves with costs. What costs, and what kind of shortest-path problem is that?
u -> v costs 0 and v -> u costs 1. With weights only 0 and 1, you can use a deque instead of a heap.
dist = inf, dist[start] = 0, deque [start]; pop left, relax neighbours; on improvement push to the left if the edge costs 0, to the right if it costs 1. Return dist[end]. O(V + E).
pitfalls: Plain BFS (counting edges) is wrong: a longer path can have fewer violations (example 3).
A vertex may be pushed more than once; relax only on a strict improvement.
